paras: The Dover Center lynch hunt for Frank Radlidge was a pursuit in late May 1882 at Dover Center, Olmsted County, Minnesota, in which a crowd sought to lynch a sixteen-year-old youth accused of assaulting a four-year-old girl. Radlidge escaped, and about a week later the Bismarck Tribune reported that the assault story had been a canard.

According to a Rochester dispatch dated May 31, Frank Radlidge was accused of enticing Minnie Harvey, aged four, into a granary near the Harvey house and assaulting her there. The dispatch said that Mrs. Harvey heard a noise, opened the granary door, and saw him holding his hand over the girl's mouth, and that the child was confined to her bed for several days.

Radlidge fled as soon as he was discovered. Within a short time a crowd was hunting him "with the full intent of lynching him," but he eluded them and escaped. Der Nordstern of St. Cloud likewise reported that he had fled with citizens behind him.

No report of his capture, arrest, or trial was found. On June 9 the Bismarck Tribune's news column said the rape case reported from Dover Center "was a canard," and that the people of the village were "highly indignant."

The Bismarck Tribune first printed the Rochester dispatch on June 2 under the headline "Another Brutal Outrage," presenting the assault as fact. Der Nordstern, a German-language paper, framed the case as one of the "unnatural brutal" crimes it reported every week, called it regrettable that he had escaped, and expressed hope that the citizens would make "short process" of him if they caught him. None of the reports named the race of anyone involved, and the Tribune's retraction gave no source or detail.

The first reports treated the assault as witnessed by the child's mother, while the later Bismarck Tribune note dismissed the whole report as a canard. The place also appears as "Dover Center" in the Tribune and as "Dover City, Olmsted Co." in Der Nordstern.
